instructional_purpose: Moves the learner past one-preposition-one-gloss thinking by presenting each common genitive-assigning preposition as a set of distinguishable semantic functions, and by supplying paraphrase tests that pick one function in a given context. Case government is held constant while the semantics vary.
concepts_taught: semantic polysemy of prepositions
sense inventory for the origin-partitive preposition
sense inventory for the instrumental proclitic
sense inventory for the ablative-topic preposition
sense inventory for the dative-possessive proclitic
paraphrase tests as sense discriminators
invariance of genitive government across all senses
traditional Arabic labels for individual senses

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The preposition من, while always assigning genitive, distributes over at least four contextual senses: starting point, constitutive material, partitive portion, and explicative specification.
The proclitic بـ covers instrument or means, comitative accompaniment, causal motivation, and the introduction of an oath.
The preposition عن covers spatial or metaphorical departure, the topic of speech or inquiry, and acting in place of another party.
The proclitic لـ covers ownership, benefit or advantage, and purpose or cause.
Which sense is chosen never alters the case of the governed noun; genitive marking is invariant across senses.
The sense inventories given (four, four, three, three) are the complete inventories for these prepositions.
A بـ introducing an animate participant after a verb of bringing or presenting is comitative rather than a transitivising element.
The sense of any given occurrence is recoverable from the semantic type of the complement together with the governing predicate.

recognition_criteria: the complement names a place or a starting bound and the predicate expresses motion, indicating the origin sense
a made-of paraphrase preserves the meaning, indicating the material sense
inserting a quantity expression such as part of preserves the meaning, indicating the partitive sense
the clause specifies which aspect of an already-mentioned entity is at issue, indicating the explicative sense
the complement is a manipulable tool and the predicate is an action, indicating instrument
the complement is a co-participant present with the subject, indicating accompaniment
the complement is an event or state and the predicate is affective, indicating cause
the predicate is a verb of swearing, indicating the oath sense
the predicate is a verb of asking, speaking, or knowing, indicating the topic sense
the predicate implies discharging another party's obligation, indicating substitution
a bare noun-to-noun link with a nominal predicate, indicating ownership
the complement is a verbal noun naming a goal, indicating purpose
procedures: locate the preposition and delimit its complement
classify the complement semantically as place, substance, mass, tool, animate participant, event, or verbal noun
apply the paraphrase test attached to each candidate sense
check that the governing predicate licenses the surviving candidate
assign the sense label and verify genitive marking independently of the sense chosen
conditions: the material sense requires a substance-denoting complement under an artefact-denoting head
the partitive sense requires a mass or plural complement conceived as divisible
the oath sense requires an oath predicate, expressed or understood
the substitution sense requires an obligation or act transferable between parties
exceptions: redundant or expletive occurrences of these prepositions, which carry no independent sense, are not treated
prepositions selected lexically by a particular verb, where the sense is idiomatic rather than compositional, are not treated
with a pronominal complement no genitive exponent is visible, so the case claim is abstract there
contrasts: origin against material for the same preposition
partitive against explicative for the same preposition
instrument against cause for the instrumental proclitic
ownership against purpose for the dative proclitic
departure against topic for the ablative preposition

common_mistakes.pattern: Reading a substance-denoting complement as a place of origin.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The construction states what an artefact is made of, not a trajectory from a location.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Run the made-of paraphrase before assigning the origin sense.

common_mistakes.pattern: Rendering the instrumental proclitic with one fixed English preposition in every occurrence.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: A uniform gloss collapses a causal reading into an accompaniment or satisfaction reading and changes the proposition asserted.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Let an affective predicate together with an event-denoting complement select the causal reading.

common_mistakes.pattern: Reading the ablative preposition as physical departure when it complements a verb of asking or speaking.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Those predicate classes select the topic sense, and a departure reading yields an incoherent proposition.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Let the governing predicate class fix the sense before consulting the default gloss.

common_mistakes.pattern: Leaving the complement unmarked or marking it nominative or accusative.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Every preposition in this set assigns genitive irrespective of which sense is selected.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Separate sense selection from case assignment; the case is constant while the sense varies.

misleading_shortcuts: treating the four sense lists as exhaustive
mapping each preposition onto a single English equivalent
assuming an animate complement always signals accompaniment
assuming any abstract complement signals cause

a discrimination note under each inventory giving the paraphrase test for each sense
a token-by-token table over the lesson narrative assigning a sense label to every preposition occurrence
a set of minimal contrast pairs holding the preposition constant while varying the complement type
paradigms: sense-inventory tables, one per preposition, functioning as licensing and discrimination tables rather than inflectional paradigms
exercise_types: multiple-choice sense identification for a preposition in a given clause
free-response translation of clauses whose reading depends on the sense chosen
fill-in-the-blank selection of the preposition matching a stated meaning
selection of which candidate clause instantiates a named sense

prerequisite_knowledge: kasra and tanwin kasra as genitive exponents
basic verbs of motion, speech, and emotion
reuses_from_earlier: the closed list of common prepositions
idafa as the other major source of genitive
new_knowledge: explicit sense inventories per preposition
paraphrase-based discriminators for sense selection
the explicit separation of semantic function from case government
traditional Arabic labels for the individual senses

nahw_relevance: high + the whole lesson concerns government and the semantics of prepositional phrases
tutor_drill_relevance: high + sense selection with type-matched distractors is directly drillable and the rejected senses supply natural distractors
rich_hover_relevance: high + a hover gloss on a preposition token must commit to one sense, so discriminators are needed to avoid a generic gloss
corpus_pvn_relevance: chiefly p entries for من, بـ, عن and لـ, each requiring sense-tagged sub-glosses rather than one gloss; secondarily n entries for the governed nouns, whose case is fixed while their semantic role varies
required_evidence: per occurrence: the governing predicate, the semantic type of the complement, and the outcome of the relevant paraphrase test; the token alone never fixes the sense
uncertainty_flags: closed sense lists presented as complete while the classical inventories are longer
several in-passage sense assignments are contestable, notably comitative versus transitivising readings of the instrumental proclitic
expletive and lexically selected prepositions are absent

proposed_new_units.summary: Per-preposition table of senses with the complement-type and predicate-class features that select each sense, plus the paraphrase test that confirms it.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-n07 is scoped to a different multifunction particle, and u-n03 covers government rather than the semantic distinctions that arise under identical government.

instructional_purpose: Splits the genitive construct into a possessive or intrinsic type and a descriptive type whose head is a derived describing word, and supplies a rephrasing test that sorts a given construct into one of the two. The aim is accurate parsing of constructs whose head is an adjective or participle rather than a substantive.
concepts_taught: two-way classification of the construct into real and non-real
semantic subtypes of the real construct: ownership, part-whole, source, material, containment
derived word classes that head the non-real construct: active participle, passive participle, elative, quasi-participial adjective
the rephrasing test as classifier
invariance of genitive on the second term across both types
definiteness behaviour of the head of a construct

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The real construct expresses ownership or another intrinsic relation between two substantive nouns.
The non-real construct is headed by a derived describing word and its second term names the respect in which the description holds.
Rephrasing a construct as a definite noun followed by an agreeing adjective identifies it as the non-real type.
In both types the head may take neither the definite article nor tanwin.
The second term supplies definiteness to the whole phrase.
The relations of the real construct are enumerable as a short list of semantic labels.
Elative heads are instances of the non-real type on the same footing as quasi-participial adjectives.
The absence of non-real constructs in a narrative passage is characteristic of narrative prose as a genre.

recognition_criteria: the head is a substantive naming a thing, a part, or a product, indicating the real type
the head is morphologically a participle, an elative, or a quasi-participial adjective, indicating a candidate non-real type
the construct restates as an entity plus an adjective describing it in one respect, confirming the non-real type
the second term names a possessor, a whole, a source, or a substance, indicating the real type
the second term names a body part, faculty, or attribute domain, which is typical of the non-real type
procedures: segment the construct into head and second term
classify the head's derivational class
attempt the rephrasing into noun plus agreeing adjective
confirm genitive marking on the second term regardless of the outcome
for the real type, select the semantic subtype label
conditions: the head must appear bare of article and tanwin as the lesson states the rule
the second term must be genitive in both types
the rephrasing test presupposes that the head can predicate over the second term
exceptions: the lesson admits no exception to the article restriction, whereas standard grammatical description licenses the article on the head of the non-real type under stated conditions
chains of more than two terms are deferred to the next lesson
pronominal second terms are not treated
contrasts: real against non-real with the same second term
ownership against part-whole inside the real type
substantive-headed against participle-headed constructs
the differing English translation frames the two types take

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating every construct as an expression of ownership.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Part-whole, source, material and purely descriptive relations are all realised by the same construct shape.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Read the relation off the semantic types of the two terms rather than off the construct shape.

common_mistakes.pattern: Translating both types with the same possessive English frame.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The descriptive type asserts a quality holding in a specified respect, not a relation of belonging, so the possessive frame states a different proposition.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Once the type is classified, choose the translation frame that the type licenses.

common_mistakes.pattern: Leaving the second term unmarked for genitive in the descriptive type.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The genitive requirement holds in both types; it follows from the construct relation, not from possession.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Mark the second term genitive whenever a construct link is present, irrespective of type.

common_mistakes.pattern: Attaching the definite article to the head of a construct.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: As the lesson states the rule, the head is barred from the article in both types; note that the lesson gives this as absolute while standard grammar licenses it for the non-real type under conditions.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Let the second term carry definiteness in the real type, and treat the head-article question in the non-real type as requiring separate authority.

misleading_shortcuts: concluding non-real from an adjective-shaped head without running the rephrasing test
treating the rephrasing test as a definition of the category rather than a heuristic
reading the absence of one type in a single passage as evidence about a genre
assuming the non-real type confers definiteness on its head the way the real type does
worked_analysis_stages: a relation-type table for the real construct pairing label, traditional term, example, and gloss
an equivalence table pairing non-real constructs with their adjective-plus-noun rephrasings
a test table listing constructs with the rephrasing outcome and the resulting verdict
an inventory over the lesson narrative classifying each construct with a relation label
a supplementary list of non-real constructs grouped by the derivational class of the head
paradigms: classification tables rather than inflectional paradigms: the relation-type table for the real construct and the rephrasing-equivalence table for the non-real construct
exercise_types: multiple-choice classification of a construct into one of the two types
multiple-choice application of the rephrasing test
multiple-choice identification of the derivational class of a head
free-response translation in both directions
fill-in-the-blank supplying the classification label
vocabulary recall items
prerequisite_knowledge: the two-term construct and genitive marking
new_knowledge: the two-way classification of the construct
the rephrasing test as classifier
the criterion that the head's derivational class predicts the type
semantic subtype labels for the real construct
later_dependencies: distinguishing the construct from the accusative of specification
parsing descriptive epithets in classical prose and verse

nahw_relevance: high + construct government, definiteness behaviour, and phrase parsing
tutor_drill_relevance: high + sorting constructs into the two types is a compact drill and substantive-headed constructs supply natural distractors
rich_hover_relevance: medium-high + a hover on a construct head must say whether it possesses or describes, since the two readings yield different glosses
corpus_pvn_relevance: n entries dominate: participle-type headwords such as كاتِب and quasi-participial adjectives need a note that they may head a descriptive construct, while ordinary substantive headwords need the possession-relation labels
required_evidence: per occurrence: the derivational class of the head, whether the second term names an attribute domain, the outcome of the rephrasing test, and the definiteness marking on both terms
uncertainty_flags: the absolute ban on the article on the head conflicts with the standard licensing of the article in the non-real construct when the second term is definite
the lesson does not state that the non-real construct confers no definiteness or specification on its head
elative heads are folded into the non-real type without addressing the partitive elative
a genre claim is drawn from a single narrative passage

proposed_new_units.summary: Discriminator that classifies a construct by the derivational class of its head and the rephrasing test, and records the definiteness consequences that follow from the class.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-n03 states construct government without distinguishing the two types, and u-s03 supplies participle morphology without the syntactic consequence of a participle heading a construct.

instructional_purpose: Extends the two-term construct to chains of three or more nouns, showing that each intermediate node carries two roles at once, and fixing the case and definiteness consequences at every position in the chain.
concepts_taught: construct chains of three or more nodes
the dual role of an intermediate node
genitive on every non-initial node
article and tanwin confined to the terminal node
the head's case set by its clause role rather than by the chain
reading a chain as nested belonging outward from the head
the use of chains in legal and scientific registers

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Every node except the first is genitive as the second term of the node preceding it.
Every node except the last governs the node following it, so intermediate nodes are simultaneously head and dependent.
Only the terminal node may carry the definite article or tanwin.
The first node's case is determined by its function in the clause and not by its position in the chain.
Chain depth is in principle unbounded and four-node chains occur in ordinary scholarly prose.
A chain should be read as nesting outward from the head rather than by reversing the order of the words.
A run of consecutive nouns may be counted as a chain of that depth without first checking that every adjacency is a construct link.
Nested fractional and inheritance expressions are naturally realised as construct chains.

recognition_criteria: a run of consecutive bare nouns, each genitive after the first
absence of article and tanwin on every node but the last
a terminal node made definite by the article, by being a proper name, or by a pronominal suffix
a chain boundary where an article-bearing modifier agrees with an earlier node instead of continuing the belonging relation
procedures: identify the head, determine its clause role, and assign its case from that role
walk rightwards assigning genitive to every subsequent node
verify that no non-terminal node carries article or tanwin
confirm the definiteness marker on the terminal node
render the chain as nested belonging starting from the head
conditions: each adjacency must be a genuine construct link
the terminal node fixes the definiteness of the whole phrase
the head's case comes from outside the chain
exceptions: separation of a head from its second term is not addressed
coordination inside a chain is not addressed
a chain whose head is a descriptive rather than a substantive head is not addressed
modifiers attached to an internal node are not analysed
contrasts: two-node against three-node against four-node chains
a definite-terminated chain against an indefinite-terminated chain
a well-formed chain against the ill-formed shape with the article on an internal node
the same chain with its head in each of the three cases

common_mistakes.pattern: Placing the definite article on an intermediate node.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Only the terminal node may bear the article; an internal node is itself a head and heads are barred from it.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Locate the terminal node first and let it alone carry the definiteness of the phrase.

common_mistakes.pattern: Marking a middle node nominative because it looks like a head.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: A middle node is a dependent of the node before it, and that role fixes its case as genitive regardless of the role it also plays towards the node after it.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Assign case from the dependent role, which is the only case-assigning relation acting on the node.

common_mistakes.pattern: Translating a chain by reversing the word order.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The relation runs from head outward, so reversing produces a different nesting and a different meaning.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Translate from the head outwards, one belonging relation at a time.

common_mistakes.pattern: Assuming the head of a chain is nominative.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The head's case reflects its clause function, which may be subject, object, or the complement of a preposition.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Determine the head's clause role before assigning its case.

misleading_shortcuts: counting nouns to compute depth without checking that each adjacency is a construct link
assuming the first article-bearing word ends the chain
assuming the head is nominative by default
assuming a chain always terminates in an article rather than a proper name or a pronominal suffix

paradigms: node-role and case tables indexed by position for chains of length three and four
exercise_types: multiple-choice on the case of a named node
multiple-choice on which node may take the article
multiple-choice identification of the ill-formed chain among candidates
multiple-choice on the dual role of a middle node
free-response translation of chains
fill-in-the-blank completing a chain with the correct form
fill-in-the-blank naming the case of non-initial nodes

prerequisite_knowledge: the case roles of subject, object, and complement of a preposition
reuses_from_earlier: construct basics and genitive marking from the preceding lesson
definiteness transmitted by the second term
new_knowledge: recursion of the construct beyond two terms
the simultaneous double role of intermediate nodes
definiteness restricted to the terminal node

later_dependencies: parsing long nominal phrases in legal and scientific prose
attachment ambiguity between a chain and a following modifier
annotation of construct depth in a corpus

tutor_drill_relevance: high + node-role and case assignment over synthetic chains of increasing depth is a cleanly generable drill

required_evidence: per occurrence: the full extent of the chain, verification that every adjacency is a construct link rather than a modifier, and the definiteness marker on the terminal node

proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-n03 states construct government for a two-term pair but not the position-indexed definiteness and case licensing that a chain of depth n requires.

instructional_purpose: Presents a single-letter connective proclitic as a five-way ambiguous element, contrasts it with the neutral connective that carries no ordering, and ties one of its readings to a mood change on the verb that follows.
concepts_taught: five functions of the connective proclitic with their traditional labels
contrast with the neutral coordinating particle
ordering plus immediacy as the coordinating semantics
subjunctive licensing under the causal reading
the environments that require the connective in a conditional apodosis
the reading that presupposes an unstated antecedent condition
the resumptive reading that opens a new sentence

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The connective conveys ordering with immediacy, whereas the neutral coordinating particle conveys neither order nor immediacy.
Under the causal reading, an imperfect verb following the connective is put in the subjunctive.
The environments licensing the causal reading are imperative, prohibition, negation, question, and wish.
A conditional apodosis requires the connective when it is nominal, future-marked, imperative, prohibitive, or introduced by certain particles.
A clause-initial connective whose trigger is unexpressed signals an elided antecedent condition.
A worked token is labelled causal with subjunctive although the verb shape cited is the apocopated answer to a command.
A connective supplying a reason after a prohibition is an instance of the elided-condition reading rather than the causal-justificatory reading.
The presence of the connective after an imperative implies subjunctive marking on the following verb.
The subjunctive outcome after the causal reading is described with case terminology rather than mood terminology.

recognition_criteria: two eventive predicates in narrative succession with no gap between them, indicating the coordinating reading
a request-type or negative clause before the connective together with a subjunctive exponent on the following imperfect verb, indicating the causal reading
a conditional protasis before the connective and an apodosis that cannot itself be an apocopated verb clause, indicating the apodosis connective
a clause-initial connective whose trigger is absent from the text, indicating the elided-condition reading
a new sentence with no grammatical dependency on what precedes, indicating the resumptive reading
procedures: identify what precedes the connective: a clause, a request, a negation, a conditional protasis, or nothing
inspect the mood exponent on any following imperfect verb
if a conditional protasis precedes, test whether the apodosis is of a type that forces the connective
if no trigger is expressed, consider the elided-condition reading before defaulting to resumption
assign the function label and record the mood consequence it entails
conditions: the subjunctive requires the causal reading and a preceding pure request or negation
the apodosis connective is required only when the apodosis cannot stand as an apocopated verb clause
the coordinating reading requires two coordinated elements of the same syntactic type
exceptions: the apodosis connective is optional when the apodosis is itself an apocopated verb clause
the resumptive reading carries no mood consequence at all
not every English coordinating conjunction corresponds to this connective
contrasts: this connective against the neutral coordinating particle
the causal reading with subjunctive against the coordinating reading whose mood is inherited from context
apodosis contexts where the connective is required against those where it is optional
the elided-condition reading against the resumptive reading

common_mistakes.pattern: Leaving the following verb in the indicative after the causal reading.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Under that reading the connective licenses the subjunctive, so an indicative exponent signals a different analysis than the one intended.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Once the preceding clause is identified as a request or a negation and the relation is result, mark the verb subjunctive.

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating this connective as interchangeable with the neutral coordinating particle.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The neutral particle asserts nothing about order, while this one asserts that the second event follows the first without delay.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Use this connective only when ordering, causation, or response is actually intended.

common_mistakes.pattern: Omitting the connective before a conditional apodosis that requires it.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: An apodosis that is nominal, future-marked, or imperative cannot attach directly to the protasis, so the result is ungrammatical.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Check the syntactic type of the apodosis before deciding whether the connective may be dropped.

common_mistakes.pattern: Using this connective wherever English would use a coordinating conjunction.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: It adds ordering or causal content that the English conjunction does not carry, so the translation over-asserts.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Default to the neutral particle and switch only when sequence, cause, or response is intended.

common_mistakes.pattern: Failing to recognise the reading that presupposes an unstated condition.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: A clause-initial occurrence that answers an unasked question is analysed as coordination, which leaves the clause without a coordinand.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: When no expressed trigger precedes, consider an elided antecedent before assigning coordination.

misleading_shortcuts: assuming a connective after an imperative always entails the subjunctive
assuming the connective always means and then
assuming any clause-initial occurrence is the elided-condition reading
describing the mood change as a change of case

instructional_purpose: Teaches a verbal particle whose reading is selected locally by the tense class of the verb immediately following it, with a secondary reading noted on each side and an explicit statement that the particle governs nothing.
concepts_taught: a particle restricted to verbal complements
certainty and completion with a perfect verb
weakened assertion with an imperfect verb
recency as a secondary reading with the perfect
frequency as a secondary reading with the imperfect
absence of any mood or case effect
the adjacency requirement between particle and verb
correspondence with the English perfect and with English modals

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The particle attaches only to verbs and never directly to a noun.
With a perfect verb the particle asserts that the event was realised and is complete.
With an imperfect verb the particle weakens the assertion to possibility.
The traditional label for the imperfect-side reading is equated with the English modals may and might.
The particle induces no change of mood on the verb that follows it.
The particle must stand immediately before the verb it modifies.
The emphatic variant formed with the oath prefix differs from the plain particle only in strength.
The possibility reading and the frequency reading with the imperfect share one form and are separated only by discourse genericity.
The reading is determined by the tense class of the immediately following token.

recognition_criteria: a perfect verb immediately after the particle, indicating certainty and completion
an imperfect verb immediately after the particle, indicating possibility
a generic statement about a type of person or a habitual truth, indicating the frequency reading
an utterance anchored at the moment the event occurs, indicating the recency reading
a noun immediately after the particle, indicating that either the analysis or the identification of the particle is wrong
procedures: locate the particle
determine the tense class of the token immediately following
assign the primary reading from the tense class
check the surrounding context for the applicable secondary reading
translate with the English aspect or modal that matches the assigned reading
conditions: the particle must be adjacent to its verb
the following token must be a verb
the frequency reading requires a generic statement
the recency reading requires an utterance anchored at the moment of the event
exceptions: the particle is optional and its absence does not negate the meaning of the clause
the emphatic variant behaves as a separate item
neither reading licenses any mood change on the verb
contrasts: perfect complement against imperfect complement with the same verb
certainty against possibility

common_mistakes.pattern: Translating the particle the same way regardless of the tense of its verb.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The two tense environments produce opposite modal force, so a fixed translation asserts certainty where the text asserts possibility or the reverse.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Determine the tense class of the following verb before choosing an English rendering.

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating the plain particle and its emphatic variant as one item.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The emphatic variant carries added force and belongs to a different environment.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Keep the two entries separate and note that the strength relation asserted between them is a simplification.

common_mistakes.pattern: Assuming the particle is required in order to express a completed past event.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: A bare perfect verb already states a completed event; the particle adds emphasis rather than basic tense meaning.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Treat the particle as an optional emphasis marker, not as a tense exponent.

common_mistakes.pattern: Overlooking the frequency reading on the imperfect side.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: In generic statements the intended sense is occasional occurrence rather than possibility, and the modal rendering misstates the claim.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Check whether the clause is generic before defaulting to the possibility reading.

common_mistakes.pattern: Separating the particle from its verb.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The particle takes an immediately adjacent verbal complement, and intervening material breaks the relation.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Place the particle directly before the verb it modifies.

misleading_shortcuts: giving the particle one English gloss
assuming any imperfect complement means might
treating the particle as a past tense marker
assuming certainty and recency are freely interchangeable readings

instructional_purpose: Introduces the phonological contrast between pharyngealised and plain consonants, fixes the membership of the emphatic set and of the wider heavy set, and shows that the contrast carries meaning and colours neighbouring vowels.
concepts_taught: pharyngealisation as an articulatory process
the four-member emphatic set and its plain counterparts
three further heavy letters that are not members of the emphatic set
the traditional mnemonic collecting all seven heavy letters
minimal pairs as evidence that the contrast is meaning-bearing
vowel colouring and its spread across a word
articulatory instructions for producing emphasis
regional and social variation in realisation

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Four consonants form the emphatic set, each paired with a plain counterpart.
Three further letters are heavy by depth of articulation but are not members of the emphatic set, and all seven are collected by a traditional mnemonic phrase.
The emphatic contrast is meaning-bearing, evidenced by minimal pairs across all four pairings.
Emphatic consonants lower and back neighbouring vowels and the effect can spread across a whole word.
A common agricultural noun is presented as containing an emphatic letter in one table and as a plain-consonant word in another.
Rural speakers maintain stronger emphatic articulation than urban speakers.
Dialect realisations of the two similar emphatics include merger and a lateral articulation.
In the classical description one of the two similar emphatics is a stop and the other a fricative.
For learners, preserving the contrast matters more than matching any particular phonetic realisation.

recognition_criteria: orthographic membership in the four-letter emphatic set
auditory darkening of a vowel adjacent to the consonant
a change of meaning when the plain counterpart is substituted
deep place of articulation for the three additional heavy letters
absence of any plain counterpart for the three additional heavy letters
procedures: place the tongue as for the plain articulation
raise the back of the tongue toward the pharynx
tense the pharynx slightly so the sound is lowered
check that neighbouring vowels have darkened
test the result against the plain counterpart word for a meaning difference
conditions: the contrast is only meaningful where a plain counterpart exists
the three additional heavy letters have no light counterpart and are always heavy
vowel colouring is a phonetic consequence and leaves the orthography unchanged
exceptions: two of the emphatics lack a plain counterpart for some of the items the lesson lists
several modern dialects neutralise part of the contrast
the mnemonic covers the seven heavy letters, not the four-member emphatic subset
contrasts: each emphatic against its plain counterpart across four pairings
the emphatic subset against the wider heavy set
bright against dark realisation of the same short vowel
rural against urban realisation
the two similar emphatics distinguished by manner of articulation

common_mistakes.pattern: Producing an emphatic consonant as its plain counterpart.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The contrast is meaning-bearing, so the substitution yields a different word rather than an accented version of the same word.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Raise the back of the tongue and darken the segment so the contrast is audible.

common_mistakes.pattern: Exaggerating emphasis until the sound is distorted.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Emphasis is a change of quality within the segment, not a different segment, and over-articulation is as unintelligible as neutralisation.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Aim for a darkening of quality rather than a maximal constriction.

common_mistakes.pattern: Producing an emphatic consonant with an undarkened neighbouring vowel.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The vowel colouring is part of the cue set listeners use, so an undarkened vowel weakens the perceived contrast.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Let the neighbouring vowel lower and back along with the consonant.

common_mistakes.pattern: Merging the two similar emphatics.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: They differ in manner in the classical description even where modern dialects have merged them, and formal registers keep them apart.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Keep the stop and the fricative distinct when reading in a formal register.

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating minimal pair members as homophones.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The pairs differ in exactly the feature under study and denote unrelated things.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Use minimal pairs as the diagnostic that the contrast has been acquired.

misleading_shortcuts: treating emphasis as ornamental rather than contrastive
conflating the heavy set with the emphatic subset
assuming the letter shape predicts realisation uniformly across dialects
assuming vowel colouring is confined to the immediately adjacent vowel

instructional_purpose: Fixes the behaviour of the cardinal numerals from one to ten: ordinary agreement for the first two, inverse gender agreement for three to ten, a construct whose second term is a genitive plural, and the anomalous behaviour of eight with feminine counted nouns.
concepts_taught: ordinary agreement and post-nominal position for the numerals one and two
inverse gender agreement for the numerals three to ten
gender computed from the singular of the counted noun
the counted noun as genitive plural second term of a construct
the numeral's own case determined by its clause role
diptote endings on some counted nouns
defective-noun behaviour of the feminine form of eight

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The numerals one and two agree in gender with the counted noun and follow it as adjectives.
The numerals three to ten take the gender opposite to that of the singular of the counted noun.
The polarity is computed from the gender of the singular, not from the shape of the plural actually used.
The numeral and the counted noun form a construct, so the counted noun is a genitive plural.
The counted noun takes kasra when triptote and fatha when diptote.
The numeral takes its case from its clause role while the counted noun remains genitive.
The feminine form of eight behaves as a defective noun, losing its final glide in the indefinite nominative and genitive.
The definite construction offered for eight places an article-bearing numeral before an article-bearing noun.
One worked example is filed under the accusative heading while its own gloss identifies it as governed by a preposition and therefore genitive.
Any plural of the counted noun is equally acceptable with three to ten.
An analysis line names a numeral different from the one appearing in its own example.

recognition_criteria: a bare numeral immediately followed by a bare plural in the genitive, indicating the construct numeral phrase
presence or absence of the feminine ending on the numeral relative to the gender of the counted singular, confirming polarity
a numeral standing after its noun and agreeing with it, indicating one or two
a numeral missing its final glide, indicating the defective feminine form of eight
fatha rather than kasra on the counted noun, indicating a diptote plural
procedures: identify the singular of the counted noun and determine its gender
select the numeral form of the opposite gender for three to ten, or the agreeing form for one and two
put the counted noun in the plural and mark it genitive
choose kasra or fatha as the genitive exponent according to triptote or diptote class
mark the numeral for the case its own clause role requires
apply defective-noun endings when using the feminine form of eight
conditions: polarity applies only to the numerals three to ten
the counted noun must be plural and never singular or dual with three to ten
the construct requires the numeral to be bare of article and tanwin
diptote marking applies only to counted nouns of the relevant patterns
exceptions: one and two fall outside the polarity rule and follow their noun
the feminine form of eight is defective
numerals eleven and above follow rules explicitly deferred to later lessons
the numeral's own case is external to the construct and varies freely
contrasts: one and two against three to ten in both agreement and position
masculine against feminine counted nouns for the same numeral
triptote against diptote counted nouns in genitive exponent
eight against the other numerals in the three-to-ten band
the same numeral phrase with the numeral in each of the three cases

common_mistakes.pattern: Applying ordinary gender agreement to the numerals three to ten.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: That band requires the opposite gender, so an agreeing form is ungrammatical rather than merely marked.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Compute the gender of the counted singular and select the opposite form.

common_mistakes.pattern: Using a singular or dual counted noun with three to ten.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The construct in this band requires a plural second term.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Pluralise the counted noun before entering it into the construct.

common_mistakes.pattern: Marking the counted noun nominative.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: It is the second term of a construct and therefore genitive irrespective of the numeral's own case.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Mark the second term genitive and mark the numeral separately from its clause role.

common_mistakes.pattern: Handling one and two by the rules of three to ten.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The first two agree and follow the noun as adjectives while the higher band reverses and precedes in a construct, so the two patterns differ in agreement, order, and government.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Split the numeral inventory into the two bands before applying any rule.

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating the feminine form of eight like the other numeral forms.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: It inflects as a defective noun, so its final glide appears and disappears with case and definiteness.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Apply the defective-noun endings to that form specifically.

misleading_shortcuts: matching the numeral to the shape of the plural instead of the gender of the singular
assuming kasra is always the genitive exponent on the counted noun
assuming the numeral is nominative by default
extending inverse agreement beyond ten

instructional_purpose: Assembles previously taught grammar into a reading procedure: recover the unwritten short vowels of unpointed text from syntactic position, word pattern, particle restrictions, and context, applied to the sentence as a whole rather than word by word.
concepts_taught: why running text is written without vowel marks
case prediction from syntactic role
word pattern recognition for identifying word class
particles as category filters on the following token
homograph disambiguation from surrounding structure
a stepwise reading procedure
shape recognition for high-frequency function words

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The syntactic role of a word determines its case ending and therefore its final vowel.
Word patterns identify word class and derivational category.

Certain particles restrict the category of the following token: the emphatic verbal particle takes only a verb, the past negative takes only an apocopated verb, the topic-marking particle takes an accusative noun, and prepositions take a genitive noun.
Context eliminates the homograph readings that a bare consonant skeleton would otherwise permit.
Reading the whole sentence before committing to any vocalisation is the correct order of operations.
The mapping from pattern to word class given in the tables is one to one.
A named consonant skeleton is more frequently read as a noun than as a verb in everyday text.
A category-restricting particle plus a consonant skeleton uniquely fixes the vocalisation of the following word.

recognition_criteria: presence of a category-restricting particle immediately before an ambiguous skeleton
presence of the definite article, marking the word as a noun or adjective and blocking tanwin
match between a candidate pattern and the skeleton's letter count and long-vowel positions
position immediately after a verb, indicating the agent and hence the nominative
position immediately after a preposition or as the second term of a construct, indicating the genitive
semantic coherence of a candidate reading within the clause
procedures: scan the sentence for particles, for the article, and for likely verbs
classify the sentence as verbal or nominal from its opening element
assign grammatical roles and the cases those roles entail
match each ambiguous skeleton against the candidate patterns
eliminate candidates that violate a particle restriction or the required case
read aloud with the predicted vowels and test whether the meaning coheres
revise the assignment if the meaning fails
conditions: the procedure presupposes knowledge of the case system, the pattern inventory, and the government of the common particles
it operates over a whole sentence, not over an isolated word
it presupposes that the text is grammatically well formed
exceptions: voice ambiguity between active and passive is not resolved by the procedure
the internal stem vowels of an unfamiliar lexeme are not recoverable from structure alone
genuinely ambiguous structures receive no resolution policy
pausal reading suppresses the very endings the procedure predicts, which the lesson does not address
contrasts: pointed against unpointed text
a word read in isolation against the same word read in a sentence
two-way against three-way homograph sets
frequency-based guessing against structure-based prediction

common_mistakes.pattern: Vocalising each word before understanding the structure of the sentence.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Most endings are determined by grammatical role, which is only available once the sentence is parsed.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Parse first, then assign the endings the parse entails.

common_mistakes.pattern: Ignoring the category restriction imposed by a preceding particle.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Those particles admit only one category, so a reading that violates the restriction is excluded before any other consideration.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Apply particle restrictions as the first filter over candidate readings.

common_mistakes.pattern: Choosing the most frequent reading of a skeleton against a particle restriction.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Frequency is a prior over the lexicon, while the restriction is a hard constraint imposed by the immediate context.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Let structural constraints override lexical frequency.

common_mistakes.pattern: Marking the second term of a construct with a nominative ending.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The construct relation assigns genitive to the second term, so the nominative signals a parse that the structure does not support.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Detect construct links during the parse and mark their second terms genitive.

common_mistakes.pattern: Misidentifying the sentence type from its opening element.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Verbal and nominal openings distribute roles differently, so misidentification propagates wrong cases across the whole clause.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Classify the opening element before assigning any role.

misleading_shortcuts: guessing the commonest reading first and checking afterwards
assuming one pattern maps to exactly one word class
assuming the first word of a sentence is always a verb
treating ending prediction as guesswork rather than as inference from structure

proposed_new_units.summary: Ordered pipeline resolving an unpointed consonant skeleton by applying particle category filters, then syntactic-role case prediction, then pattern matching, then a semantic coherence check, recording which filter decided the reading.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: the individual units supply the case system, particle behaviour, and the pattern inventory separately; none states the order in which they apply or what to do when two of them conflict.
